tagline: A fist-sized ambush with a glowing lure
summary: Also called the black seadevil, this small, velvety-black anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of a cavernous, needle-toothed mouth. The light comes from bacteria living inside the lure. Females reach about 18 cm; the dwarf males are under 3 cm and live independently.
ability: bacterial light lure and an expandable stomach

stats.size: Females up to about 18 cm; males about 3 cm
stats.depth: Usually 100–1,500 m; recorded to about 4,500 m
stats.range: Tropical to temperate waters of all oceans
stats.diet: Small fishes and crustaceans; can swallow prey longer than itself

facts.title: Borrowed light
facts.text: The female's 'fishing rod' is the first ray of her dorsal fin. Its tip, the esca, is a sac packed with light-producing bacteria, so the fish doesn't make the glow itself—its microbial partners do.

facts.title: Fishing, not chasing
facts.text: Rather than spending energy hunting, the angler hangs in the dark with its lure lit and waits. When a small fish or crustacean comes close, the huge mouth and sharp teeth snap shut.

facts.title: A stretchy stomach
facts.text: Its stomach stretches enormously. A 6.6 cm humpback anglerfish was found with a roughly 24 cm viperfish inside it—prey more than three times its own length.

facts.title: Dwarf, but not a parasite
facts.text: Males are tiny and, like other dwarf anglerfish males, find females by following their scent. Unlike some anglerfish whose males fuse permanently to the female, Melanocetus males are non-parasitic and stay free-living.

facts.title: Black as ink
facts.text: Deep-sea anglerfishes have dark skin that absorbs light—an ultra-black camouflage that helps mask their presence.

image.alt: Black-and-white engraving of an anglerfish with a round, swollen belly, a huge gaping mouth lined with thin needle-like teeth, and a slender rod with a small knob rising from its head.
image.caption: The original 1864 illustration of the species, drawn by G. H. Ford for Albert Günther's description in the Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London.
image.creator: George Henry Ford (via Biodiversity Heritage Library)

notes: Hero is a historical scientific illustration (Günther 1864 type description, PZSL) because the only real photograph on Commons (NOAA trawl specimen, used as gallery alt-1) is cluttered and does not show the lure. Rejected: NHM London display models (Commons 'Hal - Melanocetus johnsonii' and 'Melanocetus johnsonii.00x' files — these are models, not specimens) and 'Rape abisal, Greg Dykstra' (an artwork of a different-looking anglerfish). Lure/bioluminescent-bacteria and ultra-black-skin facts come from MBARI's order-level page and apply to deep-sea anglerfishes generally. The 2014 MBARI ROV video of a live Melanocetus in Monterey Canyon is often cited as a first; sources only identify it to genus, so it is not used. Common names also include 'black seadevil' and 'humpback blackdevil'.
